It distinguishes itself from static spatial filters by leveraging motion vectors to blend frames, and from pure stochastic sampling methods by focusing on temporal accumulation rather than single-sample unbiased estimation [S1, unofficial][S3, book].

The claim is partially supported. Source [S1] explicitly supports the part about distinguishing from static spatial filters by 'leveraging motion vectors to blend frames' (via temporal reprojection). However, Source [S3] describes stochastic sampling as providing 'unbiased results' in the converged image, which contradicts the claim's implication that stochastic methods do not focus on unbiased estimation (or that the distinction is based on avoiding single-sample unbiased estimation). Furthermore, Source [S3] does not mention 'temporal accumulation' as a distinguishing feature of stochastic sampling; it focuses on replacing trilinear lookups with single samples for speed. Therefore, while the first half of the claim is supported by S1, the second half regarding the distinction from stochastic methods is not supported or is contradicted by the provided evidence.
